assessment.rationale: This variant matches the scenario well at the carriage boundary: lower layers can keep condition-bearing bytes opaque, preserve exact bytes, and fail explicitly on unknown pCIDs. It is only a partial end-to-end answer, though, because unsigned v0 does not itself make the condition object authentic, current, or auditable enough to avoid accidental promise violations.
strengths: Unknown-pCID handling explicitly permits exact store-and-forward of opaque bytes without speculative parsing.
The [pcid, payload] boundary is very clear about what lower layers may carry versus what higher layers must interpret.
Canonical DAG-CBOR bytes and payload-level external/content-addressed references give higher layers a plausible place to attach verifiable condition material.
weaknesses: The base envelope has no required signature or integrity protection.
The spec does not define how an opaque condition object becomes verifiable to carriers or later auditors.
Conditional-release semantics and peer-local promise accounting are left outside the envelope.
risks: Opaque condition references can be replayed, swapped, or stale unless higher layers bind them cryptographically to the promised release conditions.
A node may be able to prove it carried bytes, but not that any release decision was actually authorized.
Long-term verification depends on preserving pCID interpretation material and whatever external authentication layer is used.
open_questions: What exact mechanism makes a geofencing condition reference verifiable when intermediary layers do not understand its semantics?
What local record should Bob keep to show he only stored or forwarded opaque material rather than authorizing release?
How are pCID handlers, spec snapshots, and authentication evidence preserved across long-term protocol evolution?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
